stories.title: Chagossians Forcibly Displaced to Seychelles
stories.description: The Facebook publication characterizes Harold Wilson's authorization of the British Indian Ocean Territory on 8 November 1965 as the beginning of the forced removal of the Chagossian population. It says that over the following few years the population was forcibly transferred from the Chagos archipelago to Seychelles, and that the largest island was leased to the United States for a military base.

publications.title: an island for no one  #Mauritius #Chagossians #history #army
publications.text:
An Island for No One: the true story of the Chagos Islands, the British Indian Ocean Territory, and the secret behind Diego Garcia, one of the most strategic US military bases on Earth.

Imagine an island chain where nobody is allowed to live. Not because it is empty, but because Britain made it that way. In the 1960s, the United States wanted a military base on a territory with no population and no pressure for independence. Britain’s solution was to make the people who already lived there disappear from the legal record.

The Chagossians were a real society, with their own Creole language, their own food, their own homes, and families going back six to eight generations. They were forced onto boats and dumped in Mauritius and Seychelles with almost no support. Internal British Foreign Office documents show officials knew exactly what they were doing and wrote about maintaining “the fiction” that the islanders were not permanent residents.

In this video you will learn:

Why the British Indian Ocean Territory is not really British
How Britain depopulated the Chagos Islands and exiled the Chagossians
What the International Court of Justice ruled about the Chagos Archipelago
Why the UK and Mauritius handover deal is stuck in limbo
How a British judge declared the ban on living in the territory unlawful
Why Diego Garcia matters so much for US military power and B-2 bomber operations

Today the territory must be returned to Mauritius because the islanders’ right to self-determination was ignored in the past, yet it may not be returned because of those same rights today. Only a few hundred Chagossians who lived on the islands are still alive to see how it ends.

🔔 Subscribe to CHOKE THEORY for more untold history, geopolitics explained, and stories they never taught you in school. Turn on notifications so you never miss a new video.

#ChagosIslands #DiegoGarcia #Geopolitics #UntoldHistory #Shorts

On this day, 8 November 1965, Harold Wilson, the "socialist" Labour prime minister, authorised the establishment of the British Indian Ocean Territory. 
This was the first act in the ethnic cleansing of the Chagos archipelago. Over the next few years every member of the Chagossian population was forcibly removed from their home, never to return. 
One foreign office official wrote to diplomat Dennis Greenhill, saying: “We must surely be very tough about this. The object of the exercise was to get some rocks which will remain ours. There will be no Indigenous population except seagulls." Greenhill replied: "Along with the birds go some few Tarzans or Men Fridays". 
The Indigenous people were allowed to take just one suitcase each before being forcibly transferred to the Seychelles, and any pets were destroyed. 
The purpose of this ethnic cleansing was so that government could lease the largest island to the United States for $1 per year for them to establish a military base.
More information, sources and map: https://stories.workingclasshistory.com/article/10846/ethnic-cleansing-of-the-chagos-islands

stories.title: Judicial Appointment Scrutiny Urged After Govinden Resignation
stories.description: A Facebook reflection published on 9 November 2026 responds to the Office of the President’s announcement on 6 November 2026 that Chief Justice Rony Govinden had resigned. It calls for transparency, independent scrutiny and accountability in judicial appointments, including scrutiny of any possible appointment of Govinden as a Justice of Appeal; it says concerns should be investigated, not treated as established facts, and does not report that a new appointment occurred.

publications.text:
THE LIGHTHOUSE DOESN'T BELONG TO THE KEEPER
OracleMaster  Reflection :

On 6 November 2026, the Office of the President announced the resignation of Chief Justice Rony Govinden. A chapter has closed at the highest level of Seychelles' judiciary.

But the question isn't simply who comes next. The more important question is:

What do we want justice to look like moving forward?

THE LIGHTHOUSE PRINCIPLE

A lighthouse doesn't exist to honour its keeper. It exists so that every ship can trust the light it provides.

When a lighthouse keeper steps down, a wise harbour doesn't simply hand over the keys to the next person. It inspects the lamp, cleans the glass and asks whether the light remains trustworthy.

Chief Justice Govinden's resignation presents Seychelles with precisely that opportunity.

The strength of a judiciary isn't measured by the names displayed on its doors, but by the confidence the public places in its independence, integrity and impartiality.

🌱 WHY THIS MOMENT IS AN OPPORTUNITY

✨ An opportunity to reset standards, not merely change personnel.

✨ An opportunity to strengthen the systems that safeguard fairness and accountability.

✨ A reminder that no individual officeholder is greater than the institution they serve.

A resignation should not become a revolving door. Mr Govinden's departure could instead become a doorway to institutional renewal.

 THE CORE MESSAGE

1. Transparency over assumptions.

Concerns raised over the years deserve independent scrutiny. They should neither be buried nor presented as established facts without proper investigation.

2. Institutions over individuals.

There has been public discussion about whether Mr Govinden might seek another judicial appointment, such as Justice of Appeal. Any such appointment should be examined against the principles of public confidence, institutional integrity and judicial independence.

3. Impartiality must not only exist; it must be seen.

Even where no wrongdoing has been established, the justice system must maintain public confidence. Potential conflicts of interest and even the appearance of undue influence must be carefully addressed.

4. Accountability applies to everyone.

Oversight bodies and the Constitutional Appointments Authority must be prepared to face the same level of scrutiny they are expected to apply to others.

THE VISION

Imagine a Seychelles where every judicial appointment is open to scrutiny, where oversight institutions act with courage and independence, and where citizens can proudly say:

"Our courts belong to the people."

This is not about condemning anyone without evidence. It is about demanding transparency, independent review and the highest standards of public accountability.

The departure of a Chief Justice should mark the beginning of a new chapter, not simply the recycling of leadership while legitimate questions remain unanswered.

That's not a dream. That's a decision.

💬 YOUR TURN

What's the ONE standard you believe every judicial appointment in Seychelles should meet?

Drop your answer below. 👇

🔁 Share if you believe justice should shine brighter than any name.

stories.title: Seychelles Seeks Russian Medical Training Cooperation
stories.description: Health Minister Marvin Nolan Fanny told African Initiative that Seychelles is interested in expanding medical cooperation with Russia, including specialist training, professional exchanges and treatment of combat-related trauma. He made the remarks on 3 November 2026 at a reception aboard the Russian frigate Marshal Shaposhnikov in the port of Victoria (Seychelles), citing the limited range of clinical cases local doctors encounter and the potential value of exchanging expertise.

publications.text:
🇸🇨🇷🇺 Seychelles interested in developing cooperation with Russia in military and civilian medicine

Seychelles is interested in expanding cooperation with Russia in military and civilian medicine, including the training of medical specialists, exchange of professional experience and treatment of traumatic injuries in combat conditions.

Health Minister Marvin Nolan Fanny told African Initiative about this on 3 November during a reception aboard the Russian Pacific Fleet frigate Marshal Shaposhnikov in the port of Victoria.

According to the minister, Seychelles has a relatively small population, which means that local doctors have fewer opportunities to encounter a wide range of clinical cases. Cooperation with countries that have greater medical resources and experience would help Seychelles specialists develop their professional skills.

Mr Fanny particularly highlighted the importance of exchanging experience between the military forces of the two countries in the fields of military medicine, battlefield medicine and trauma treatment.

The minister expressed confidence that professional exchanges could become a foundation for closer cooperation between Russian and Seychellois medical specialists.

🌍 African Initiative continues to cover the development of Russia–Seychelles cooperation.

#Seychelles #Russia #Healthcare #MilitaryMedicine #RussiaAfrica #AfricanInitiative

Seychelles is interested in developing co-operation with Russia in military and civilian medicine, including specialist training, sharing experience in trauma treatment and providing medical assistance in combat conditions. Seychelles Health Minister Marvin Nolan Fanny told African Initiative this on 3 November at a reception aboard the Russian Pacific Fleet frigate Marshal Shaposhnikov.

🔸According to Fanny, the small population of Seychelles means that local medical professionals encounter a limited number of clinical cases. Training and exchanging experience with countries that have greater resources and larger patient numbers therefore help doctors improve their professional skills.

💬“Most of our professionals go and train overseas, at least to degree level. <…> It’s always helpful to have exposure to other nations who are more experienced in terms of the number of patients they treat. And it’s good to have exchanges, especially between our military forces, so as to learn what is currently happening in terms of military medicine, battlefield medicine and trauma,” the minister stressed.

stories.title: Seychelles Projected to Record 1.0% Real GDP Growth in 2026
stories.description: A social-media publication dated 27 October 2026 cites October 2026 IMF World Economic Outlook data, projecting Seychelles’ real GDP growth at 1.0% for 2026 and describing the tourism-heavy island economy as recovering slowly. This is a projection, not a reported realized growth outcome.

publications.text:
📉 LEAST PERFORMING AFRICAN ECONOMIES 2026.

Real-time IMF data (October 2026 World Economic Outlook)

While some African countries are among the world’s fastest-growing, others are barely moving — or even shrinking.

These projections real GDP growth in 2026:

1. 🇬🇶 Equatorial Guinea — –1.7%  

Only economy expected to contract. Declining oil production from mature fields and almost no diversification.

2. 🇸🇹 São Tomé and Príncipe — 0.4%  

Tiny island economy with high debt and very limited options beyond cocoa and tourism.

3. 🇿🇦 South Africa — 1.0%  

Biggest economy on the continent but stuck. Electricity problems, broken logistics (ports & rail), high unemployment, and weak investment.

4. 🇲🇿 Mozambique — 1.0%  

Insurgency in the north + repeated climate disasters (cyclones and floods).

5. 🇸🇨 Seychelles — 1.0%  

Tourism-heavy small island state still recovering slowly.

6. 🇱🇸 Lesotho — 1.1%  

Heavily dependent on South Africa and struggling manufacturing.

7. 🇳🇦 Namibia — 2.0%  

Soft commodity prices and fiscal pressure.

8. 🇲🇼 Malawi — 2.6%  

Forex shortages, high inflation, and climate vulnerability.

9. 🇨🇫 Central African Republic — 2.7%  

Ongoing conflict and extremely weak institutions.

10. 🇲🇺 Mauritius — 2.7%  

Mature economy facing slower tourism and financial services growth.

Poorest countries by GDP per capita (2026 IMF estimates):  

🇸🇸 South Sudan (~$488)  
🇧🇮 Burundi (~$550)  
🇨🇫 Central African Republic (~$613)  
🇲🇬 Madagascar (~$630)  
🇲🇿 Mozambique (~$635)

Main reasons behind the weak performance:  

• Over-reliance on oil or a single commodity  
• Conflict and insecurity  
• Broken infrastructure (especially power and logistics)  
• Climate shocks  
• High debt and limited policy space  

Africa’s growth is real — but it’s extremely uneven.

Which country do you think has the biggest chance of turning around?

publications.title: President Herminie Emphasises Monetary Stability as New Central Bank Governor Prepares to Take Office
publications.text:
President Herminie Emphasises Monetary Stability as New Central Bank Governor Prepares to Take Office

Maintaining monetary and financial stability remains a key priority for Seychelles, President Dr Patrick Herminie emphasised during a meeting with the newly appointed Governor of the Central Bank of Seychelles (CBS), Ms Sarah Lloyd, at State House on Wednesday afternoon.

The President formally presented Ms Lloyd with her letter of appointment ahead of her assuming office on 1 November 2026.

During their discussions, the importance of maintaining a stable financial environment and the Central Bank's role in safeguarding the country's economy were highlighted. The meeting also placed particular emphasis on the institution's responsibility to preserve price stability and sustain confidence in the financial system.

Having already undertaken a preliminary visit and held discussions with the Central Bank team, Ms Lloyd expressed confidence in the institution's capabilities and looked forward to serving the country in her new role.

President Herminie underscored the importance of continuity in the Central Bank's work as Ms Lloyd prepares to assume leadership of the institution. He wished her success in carrying out her responsibilities.

Speaking to the press following the meeting, Ms Lloyd outlined her priorities, placing particular emphasis on further developing the financial services sector while preserving financial and price stability.

“Alongside the already established priorities of the institution, my focus will be on further deepening the financial services sector, while ensuring that we preserve the stability of our financial system and maintain price stability,” she said.

Addressing questions about the independence of the Central Bank, particularly in situations where its policy direction may differ from that of government, Ms Lloyd stressed the importance of protecting the institution's autonomy and maintaining its longstanding reputation for integrity.

She acknowledged that differences in policy direction could arise but noted that constructive engagement and mutual understanding would be essential in navigating such situations.

“The Central Bank of Seychelles has a history and legacy of being a strong institution that has always delivered with integrity and independence. Continuing to maintain that reputation will be paramount in fulfilling my duties,” she stated.

Ms Lloyd further explained that stakeholder engagement would play an important role in fostering a shared understanding of policy decisions, even where differences exist between the Central Bank and government.

She noted that greater appreciation of the reasons behind differing policy positions could help both institutions identify common ground, particularly as they ultimately work towards the same broader economic objectives.

However, she maintained that the independence of the Central Bank as an institution must remain protected.

Turning to her immediate priorities upon assuming office, Ms Lloyd said her first task would be to engage with staff across the institution to better understand their needs and how they could continue working together to deliver the Central Bank's services effectively.

“I think, as with any new role, my first priority will be to engage with all the staff and take an introductory approach to understanding their needs, ensuring that I know exactly what they require going forward and how we can continue working together,” she explained.

Reflecting on her decision to accept the appointment, Ms Lloyd described her return to the Central Bank as a particularly meaningful moment in her professional career.

Having begun her career at the institution in 2007, she spent approximately 12 years serving in various capacities before moving into commercial banking.

“Although I subsequently moved into commercial banking, accepting this role really felt like coming home,” she said, describing the Central Bank as the institution where she began a career of which she remains proud.

Ms Lloyd brings extensive experience in banking, financial risk management and economic research. Prior to her appointment, she served as Chief Risk Officer of Absa Bank Zambia PLC, a position she had held since March 2022. She previously occupied the same position at Absa Bank (Seychelles) Limited between February 2019 and March 2022.

Her career at the Central Bank began as a Research Assistant before she progressed to Economist and later Senior Financial Stability Analyst. During her tenure, she established and managed the Financial Stability Unit and represented Seychelles at regional and international forums.

She holds a Master of Science in Financial Economics from City University London and a Bachelor of Science in Banking and International Finance from Cass Business School.

Her appointment comes as the Central Bank continues its mandate of safeguarding monetary and financial stability, with Ms Lloyd identifying institutional independence and further development of the financial services sector among her priorities.

Safeguarding the independence of the Central Bank of Seychelles (CBS) will remain a central priority under its new leadership, Ms Sarah Lloyd emphasised following her meeting with President Dr Patrick Herminie at State House on Wednesday afternoon.

The President formally presented Ms Lloyd with her letter of appointment, highlighting the important role of the Central Bank in safeguarding the country's economy and maintaining public confidence in the financial system.

Ms Lloyd, who brings extensive experience in banking and financial risk management, will officially assume office on 1 November 2026.

The President wished her success as she prepares to take on her new responsibilities.

stories.title: Sea Turtle Theft Case on Praslin (Seychelles)
stories.description: A Facebook publication dated 10 November 2026 reports that two sea-turtle theft cases were discovered within 24 hours; it identifies the latest as a case on Praslin (Seychelles), where the turtle was transported to Mahé (Seychelles) for medical care. The minister reminded the public that stealing sea turtles or possessing turtle meat is a serious offence under the law; the incidents’ occurrence dates are not specified.

publications.text:
BE KIND IS APPALLED BY THIS ACT OF CRUELTY.

This morning, we woke up to deeply disturbing footage circulating on social media showing the horrific abuse of a sea turtle on Praslin.

On behalf of BE KIND – Advocate for Animals, we are absolutely appalled and saddened that such cruelty can take place right under our noses in Seychelles.

There is simply no excuse for this behaviour. Our wildlife, whether on land or in our oceans, deserves protection, respect and compassion. A sea turtle is a precious part of our marine ecosystem, not an object for someone's amusement or cruelty.

We acknowledge the Seychelles Police and the Department of Environment for their intervention and the ongoing investigation, as well as the efforts being made to provide the injured turtle with specialised medical attention.

We expect this matter to be pursued to its fullest extent under the law and that the harshest penalties available are imposed if those responsible are found guilty. Acts of animal cruelty must have serious consequences. There can be no tolerance and no turning a blind eye.

We also urge anyone with information relating to this incident to come forward and assist the authorities.

As BE KIND, we will continue to stand up for those who cannot speak for themselves. Animal cruelty is not acceptable, it is not something we should become accustomed to, and it must never go unchallenged.

BE KIND. Be their voice.

Pli resan I en ka Praslin kot sa torti in bezwen ganny transporte Mahe pour swen medikal. 

Minister Lanvironnman, Klima, Lenerzi ek Resours Natirel i rapel manm piblik ki vol torti-d-mer oubyen an posesyon lavyann torti ki sa i en lofans serye anba lalwa.

stories.title: Parliamentarians Consulted on Seychelles National Youth Policy
stories.description: On 4 November 2026, Members of the National Assembly met representatives of the Ministry of Youth and Sports and the National Youth Policy Committee as part of consultations for Seychelles’ next National Youth Policy. The discussion gathered parliamentarians’ perspectives on young people’s needs, aspirations and challenges; the policy is still under development.

publications.text:
On the afternoon of Wednesday 4th November 2026, Members of the National Assembly met with representatives of the Ministry of Youth and Sports and the National Youth Policy Committee (NYPC) as part of ongoing stakeholder consultations to inform the development of Seychelles' next National Youth Policy.

The engagement formed part of preparations for the consultation phase of the policy development process and provided an opportunity for parliamentarians to contribute their perspectives on the needs, aspirations and challenges facing young people across the country.

The National Youth Policy serves as the Government's principal framework for youth development and is implemented through a multi-sectoral approach involving the Seychelles National Youth Council (SNYC) and various Ministries, Departments and Agencies. The new policy aims to build on lessons learned from the implementation of the previous policy, which covered the period 2018–2023, while responding to emerging priorities and evolving challenges affecting young people.

Emphasising the importance of evidence-based policy development, Mr. Arissol highlighted the need to ensure that future interventions are informed by the lived experiences of young people. “We need to evaluate the programmes aimed at youths which are active today and determine whether they are truly making an impact. As part of this process, we engage in sustained consultations with young people from all walks of life, including those in employment as well as those living in vulnerable situations. Their perspectives are what drive meaningful change.”

Concluding the session, Chairperson Hon. Gabriel reiterated the importance of a collaborative approach to youth development. “This has been a very fruitful discussion. As policymakers, we must come together and strategize around this common goal that we all seek to achieve, regardless of political affiliation. The development and wellbeing of our young people is a national priority that requires a collective effort. We wish the NYPC every success as it continues its work and the MYSCC looks forward to receiving the final report and recommendations arising from this important process.”

Last week marked another important step in developing our National Youth Policy.

What makes this process different is how it is being done — for the first time, young Seychellois are leading its formulation.

By the youth. For the youth. With the youth.

Our consultation with educators, lecturers and student support professionals was equally important. They work with young people every day and understand both their aspirations and the challenges they face. Their experience will be vital in shaping a policy that is practical and implementable.

My message was simple: identify the gaps, but also bring the solutions.

And to our young people: your voice matters, but so does your participation in making the policy succeed.

stories.title: German Tourist Found Dead Near Anse Coco (Seychelles) Trail
stories.description: Seychelles Police reported that a German tourist was found dead near the Anse Coco (Seychelles) trail and that an investigation was launched. The date and circumstances of the death are not specified; the report was published on 28 October 2026.

publications.text:
🔴 𝐋𝐚𝐩𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐬 𝐈 𝐤𝐨𝐧𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐦 𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐦𝐨𝐫 𝐭𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐬 𝐀𝐥𝐦𝐚𝐧. 

Lapolis in konfirmen ki sa viziter etranze ki ti ganny raporte manke lo santye Anse Coco bomaten in ganny dekouver mor ozordi apremidi, dan en landrwa andeor santye ant Petite Anse ek Anse Coco.

Dan en kominike lapolis I dir en lanket in konmanse pou etabli sirkonstans otour son lanmor an atandan rezilta letopsi.

Sa zonm Alman aze 30an, ti ariv Sesel le 25 Oktob 2026 e ti ekspekte kit pei demen le 28 Oktob 2026.

(Sours: Departman Lapolis)

PR AND CORPORATE IMAGE UNIT
27.10.2026

Kominike

Lapolis e zofisye Lazans Servis Tenny Dife ek Sovtaz baze lo La Digue in ansemoman mont en loperasyon resers ek sekour lo  Santye Anse Coco, pour rod en viziter kin ganny raporte manke.

Sa i vin apre en rapor ki lapolis tin fek resevwar ki en viziter etranze, tin kit son letablisman e prezimen nal dan santye Anse Coco.

Plis detay dan en prosen kominike. 
 
Departman Lapolis

PR AND CORPORATE IMAGE UNIT
27.10.2026

Kominike (Swivi)

Sa viziter etranze ki ti ganny raporte manke lo santye Anse Coco bomaten avek Lapolis in ganny dekouver mor ozordi apremidi, dan en landrwa andeor santye ant Petit Anse ek Anse Coco.

Sa zonm aze 30an e ki annan nasyonalite Alman, ti ganny raporte manke apre ki i ti retourn lo lans Anse Coco ver 9er diswar pour al rod en lekipman plonze ki i tin oubliye lo sa lans pli boner.

Lapolis ti mobiliz plizyer zofisye sorti Mahé pour asiste dan sa loperasyon resers, enkli bann zofisye sorti Dog Unit, Lapolis Lamarin ek lekip Drone e osi zofisye Lazans Servis Tenny Dife ek Sovtaz baze lo La Digue e lezot sivilyen ki tin osi asiste.

Sa viziter tin ariv Sesel le 25 Oktob 2026 e ti ekspekte kit pei demen le

Police Statement (Follow-up) 🚨

The foreign visitor who was reported missing to the police this morning while hiking along the Anse Coco trail has been found dead this afternoon in an area off the trail between Petit Anse and Anse Coco.

The 30-year-old German national was reported missing after returning to Anse Coco beach at around 9 p.m. to retrieve diving equipment he had left behind earlier.

The police mobilised several officers from Mahé to assist with the search operation. These included officers from the Dog Unit, the Marine Police and the Drone Team, as well as officers from the Seychelles Fire and Rescue Services based on La Digue. Several civilians also assisted in the search.

A detailed investigation has been launched to establish the circumstances surrounding his death, pending the results of a post-mortem examination.

The visitor arrived in Seychelles on 25 October 2026 and was scheduled to leave the country on 28 October 2026.

Police Department

stories.title: Western Indian Ocean Seagrass Synthesis Launched
stories.description: WIOMSA and IUCN launched the Western Indian Ocean Regional Seagrass Synthesis Report in Dar es Salaam (Tanzania) on 9 October 2026, alongside national Seagrass Status Reports and IOC Member State chapters. Seychelles' Minister for Environment, Climate, Energy and Natural Resources (Marie-May Jeremie) unveiled the publication, which the organizers describe as a scientific baseline for regional priorities and implementation of the WIO Regional Seagrass Strategy.

publications.text:
𝐊𝐌𝐅𝐑𝐈 𝐚𝐭 𝐂𝐎𝐏 12: 𝐒𝐄𝐀𝐆𝐑𝐀𝐒𝐒𝐄𝐒 𝐈𝐍 𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐖𝐄𝐒𝐓𝐄𝐑𝐍 𝐈𝐍𝐃𝐈𝐀𝐍 𝐎𝐂𝐄𝐀𝐍 𝐁𝐎𝐎𝐊 𝐋𝐀𝐔𝐍𝐂𝐇

The Kenya Seagrass Outlook, a national status report developed under the WIOMSA regional seagrass outlook process, was presented at COP12 by Senior research Scientist Ms. Lillian Daudi, bringing decades of quietly written seagrass science into one national report cementing a dedicated management framework for this ecosystem. 

The report is a call to action to a coordinated national monitoring and mapping, visibility for seagrass in policy and its implementation, practical information for managers, and recognition of communities as knowledge holders and conservation partners, and seagrass ecosystem investments that follows the evidence. 

The process was supported by IUCN in partnership with Western Indian Ocean Marine Science Association (WIOMSA) under the WIOCOR project, with policy partners Fauna & Flora and EAWLS, funded by The Pew Charitable Trusts opening the space for seagrass in national policy.

The Regional Outlook report was officially launched by the Honorable Marie-May Jeremie, Minister for Environment, Climate, Energy and Natural Resources, Seychelles and Mr. Gilles Fabrice David, Mauritius Junior Minister of Agro-Industry, Food Security, Blue Economy and Fisheries.
#arbeciii #kmfri #marineconservation #seagrass #COP12

A Landmark Achievement for Seagrasses in the Western Indian Ocean

Today at Nairobi Convention COP12 in Dar es Salaam, WIOMSA and IUCN marked a defining regional achievement with the official launch of the Western Indian Ocean Regional Seagrass Synthesis Report alongside the national Seagrass Status Reports and IOC Member State Chapters.

The milestone publication was officially unveiled by Hon. Marie-May Jeremie (Minister for Environment, Climate, Energy and Natural Resources, Seychelles & WIOMSA President) and Mr. Gilles Fabrice David (Junior Minister of Agro-Industry, Food Security, Blue Economy and Fisheries, Mauritius). 

Representing years of regional collaboration, cross-border science, and policy integration, this comprehensive body of work establishes the scientific baseline needed to shape national priorities and deliver the WIO Regional Seagrass Strategy toward biodiversity and climate commitments.

Key imperatives established by the synthesis:

•Standardized Monitoring: Moving beyond  baseline datasets to tracking long-term ecological condition and ecosystem health.

•Policy Visibility: Embedding seagrass directly into marine spatial planning, coastal development frameworks, and fisheries governance.

•Community-Led Stewardship: Recognizing coastal communities, artisanal fishers, and women gleaners as significant knowledge holders and conservation partners.

•Targeted Investment: Prioritizing the protection of intact meadows and catchment-to-sea management to drive effective blue carbon and resilience financing.

This initiative was coordinated under the WIO-COR Programme in partnership with IUCN, research institutions and regional partners.

WIOMSA and IUCN gratefully acknowledge the Commission de l'océan Indien - Indian Ocean Commission through the RECOS Project, funded by the AFD - Agence Française de Développement and the Fonds Français pour l’Environnement Mondial (FFEM), for financing the IOC Member State chapters, alongside every scientist, practitioner, and government agency whose expertise made this synthesis possible.

stories.title: Chagossians Forcibly Relocated for Diego Garcia Base
stories.description: The video alleges that a secret memo in 1966 laid the groundwork for British officials’ forced expulsion of Chagossians to clear land for a U.S. military base on Diego Garcia. It says displaced people were relocated to Mauritius and Seychelles and describes blocked medical returns and the destruction of family pets; the expulsion date is not specified. The video was published on 16 October 2026.

publications.text:
Britain removed an entire population from their islands in the Indian Ocean to make room for an American military base.

To force the last families out, officials rounded up the islanders' dogs and killed them in front of them.

The Chagos Archipelago. Between 1968 and 1973 the entire population — somewhere around fifteen hundred to two thousand people, descended from enslaved Africans brought to the islands by the French — was removed.

It was done quietly. People who left for medical treatment were told they could not return. Supply ships stopped coming. Food ran out.

And on Diego Garcia, to break the resistance of those who refused to go, officials had the islanders' dogs gassed and burned in a shed while their owners listened. It is recorded in the documents.

They were put on cargo boats, in some cases on the open deck alongside horse feed, and dumped in Mauritius and the Seychelles with nothing.

Families who had been fishermen and coconut workers for generations ended up in slums. There was a documented wave of deaths from despair in the first years.

The base is still there. The islanders have been in court almost continuously since. 

In 2019 the International Court of Justice held that the separation of the islands was unlawful and that Britain should end its administration.

In 2024 Britain agreed to transfer sovereignty to Mauritius, with the base remaining under a long lease.

Most of the people who were removed are dead. Some of the survivors are in their eighties, in Crawley and Port Louis, still asking to be allowed to go home.

publications.title: They Classified These Humans as "Seagulls" #shorts
publications.text:
In 1966, a secret memo laid the groundwork for one of the most ruthless cover-ups in modern history. 

To make way for a top-secret U.S. military base on the island of Diego Garcia, British officials quietly ordered the forced expulsion of the Chagossian people—declassifying an entire African-descended population to clear the land. 

From blocked medical returns to the systemic destruction of family pets and total forced relocation to the slums of Mauritius and the Seychelles, this is the story of the Chagos Archipelago that modern textbooks erased.

stories.title: Russia Plans Counterterrorism Assistance Expansion to Seychelles
stories.description: A Telegram publication dated 11 November 2026 reports that Russian Foreign Ministry official Peter Ilyichev said Russia’s technical assistance programme, conducted with the UN Office on Drugs and Crime to strengthen African partners’ defence, law-enforcement and justice capabilities, will expand to Seychelles and three other countries. The date of the statement and the timing or details of Seychelles’ participation are not specified.

publications.text:

Moscou fournit une assistance technique pour renforcer les capacités de défense, de maintien de l'ordre et de justice de ses partenaires africains, en collaboration avec 🇺🇳 l'Office des Nations unies contre la drogue et le crime (ONUDC), a déclaré Piotr Ilitchev 🇷🇺, lors d'un forum international sur la sécurité collective.

publications.title: Drogen-Hotspot Seychellen: Wie Heroin und Crystal Meth das Urlaubsparadies verändern | Weltspiegel
publications.text:
Die Seychellen sind für Traumstrände, türkisblaues Meer und Luxusurlaub bekannt. Doch hinter dem Urlaubsparadies verbirgt sich ein großes Problem mit harten Drogen: Heroin, Crystal Meth und andere.

Einer, der etwas verändern will, ist Kenneth. Er arbeitet seit fast zehn Jahren als Sozialarbeiter für die Regierung. Kenneth war früher selbst abhängig. Heute unterstützt er Menschen beim Versuch, aus der Drogensucht herauszukommen. Auf seiner Tour über die Insel treffen wir Abhängige und einen Dealer und erleben eine Razzia der Polizei.
Wie konnte das Urlaubsparadies zum Drogen-Hotspot werden? Wie kommen die Drogen auf die Seychellen? Und kann Kenneth Menschen aus einer Sucht befreien, die er selbst nur zu gut kennt?

stories.title: Fire Affects Private Residence in La Retraite (Seychelles)
stories.description: The Seychelles Fire and Rescue Services Agency confirmed that a fire affected a private residence in La Retraite (Seychelles), in Anse Etoile (Seychelles), during 26–31 October 2026; it was one of three house fires recorded across Mahé (Seychelles) that week. No injuries were reported, and the case is under investigation; its cause and the extent of the damage have not been disclosed.

publications.text:
Three house fires recorded across Mahé in one week

Three house fires have been recorded across Mahé this week, raising fresh concerns about fire safety in residential communities.

The Seychelles Fire and Rescue Services Agency (SFRSA) confirmed that the incidents affected a private residence at La Retraite, Anse Etoile, St Ange Housing Estate at Tamaka and the Transit Home at Barbarons, Grand Anse Mahé.

Despite the damage caused by the fires, no injuries have been reported in any of the three incidents.

The agency said all three cases are currently under investigation. However, no further details have been released about the possible causes of the fires or the extent of the damage.

The incidents serve as a reminder of the importance of fire prevention and safety measures, particularly in residential areas and public facilities.
Dife in detri en lakaz La Retraite. Sa lensidan in ganny raporte ozordi swar.

stories.title: TRNUC Victim Says Reparations Process Remains Unclear
stories.description: In an opinion published on 25 October 2026, Dorothy Chang-Him, identifying herself as the complainant in Case 001, says victims in Seychelles still lack clear answers and a timetable for reparations. She criticizes the arrangements for the Reparation Trust Fund and says her family has not received a formal state apology, arguing that official declarations of closure do not reflect victims’ unresolved claims.

By Dorothy Chang-Him (𝑫𝑪𝑯) A 𝑪𝒊𝒗𝒊𝒄 𝑽𝒐𝒊𝒄𝒆 & 𝑳𝒆𝒂𝒅𝒆𝒓 🦅🗣📢🇸🇨🌍

On 13 October 2026, Seychelles Nation published an article under the headline “Closure has finally arrived after 49 years”. I read it twice. Then I checked my letterbox, my phone and my email, because surely, if my closure had arrived, somebody would have delivered it to me...

Not so much to my surprise. Nothing. Not a call, a letter, or a knock on the door. Apparently closure was printed in a newspaper headline before anyone thought to post it to the people it belongs to.

Seeing as they say what they want, I will ask the question nobody at State House has been brave enough to answer. Who signed for it?

I have asked the same questions so many times now that I could recite them in my sleep, and some nights I do. I have consistently written. I have attended. I have sat across tables and been told my concerns are noted. What comes back are letters from a chairman acknowledging that meetings took place. But where are the answers? What was said? What was decided? And by whom?

The chairman’s response said that Case 001 had not been discussed and that nobody would represent my case without my authorisation. That still leaves my questions unanswered. What process is being developed? What decisions have been taken? How will affected families participate? An assurance about who cannot represent me is hardly an explanation of what happens next. Why are we never allowed to know the process? Surely our cases show why we do not blindly trust any process that is forced to be accepted.

An acknowledgement that a meeting happened is not information. It is a receipt for a parcel that never arrives. We speak freely anba langar. We compare notes, ask the questions and refuse to let silence pass for an answer. It has quietly become a platform where we Seychellois ask these questions and solve our own problems, in public for almost a year.

That is where we are: a stalemate. And in a stalemate the victim is expected to hold their position forever, whatever their health, bank balance, or age. Whatever the explanation for the delay, its consequences fall on families whose time is running out.

In his State of the Nation address this year, the President assured the country that "when we make a promise, we deliver." He also announced SCR20 million in the 2026 budget to begin compensating victims. How much has actually been transferred, how much has reached victims, and what remains available? A clear delivery timetable remains missing. An announced allocation does not tell a waiting family when relief will arrive.

What exactly has been delivered to us, apart from another reason to wait? A lot of promises were made in public and in private. Nothing has arrived and the distractions seem to get more attention. We are not blind; we all notice you ignoring the obvious...

From where I stand, trust the process means stay quiet, patient, broken, poor, disappointed, and one day, inevitably, be buried. Lucky for them, we are a strong people. Without that resilience, many of us would already have been pushed into the dark for good. For victims, trust the process is not a promise. It is a waiting room with no doctor.

Let me be fair, because fairness is something we were never shown. Things have happened on paper. In May this year, Bill No. 9 of 2026 was published to create a Commission for the Enforcement, Implementation and Monitoring of the TRNUC Recommendations. It subsequently became Act 10 of 2026, assented to on 19 June.
On 6 August that Commission was sworn in before President Herminie, and its chair, Mr George Bibi, said its immediate priority was to set up standard operating procedures and a framework for deciding reparations. Its mandate duration is not clear.

Your own law requires transparency and agreement with the victim on the final reparation determination. Explain how that agreement will be reached, what information we will receive, and what happens if we disagree. I speak as the complainant in Case 001. Where is the timetable for any of this?

In its announcement published on 16 October, Cabinet reported approving regulations for a Reparation Trust Fund, overseen by a Board of Trustees that the Commission proposes and the President appoints. Now picture the old boutik in your district. Imagine the shopkeeper behind the counter with the credit book. 

Only this time it is the shopkeeper who owes us, and he still holds the pen. He writes down what he owes, he decides when he has paid, and when you ask to see the page, he tells you it is being handled. That is how this arrangement looks from my side of the counter. The Commission proposes the trustees and the President appoints them, a president who has spent the best part of a year forcing us to endure his fandom over Albert René and his work. 

So, what they are telling us is the trustees pay what the Commission decides. When the State responsible for repairing the harm also appoints the people administering that repair, victims need visible safeguards. Show us the appointment criteria, conflicts-of-interest rules, funding arrangements and means of challenging decisions. Trust cannot be demanded across a counter we are not allowed to see behind. How is this transparent?

A framework, three and a half years after the TRNUC handed its final report to the former President in March 2023? It is like a man who promised to fix your leaking roof, let three rainy seasons pass, then turns up with a tape measure to ask how big the house is.

The TRNUC already heard us. It investigated. It already made its findings and recommendations. What we were promised was implementation, more than once. What we are getting is a new start dressed up as an apparent ending. How many times can the starting line be advertised as the finish?

The completion of a commission’s work cannot be presented as the completion of justice for the families still waiting. It is being re-wrapped, re-staffed and re-timed, and once again it is being done from the top of State House down to the cleaner's cupboard without one serious conversation with the people it is supposed to repair.

Then there is the Act’s promise of closure for victims and perpetrators. Victims and perpetrators, in one breath, under one blanket. This language has followed the process for years. Its age does not answer my concern. What safeguards ensure that rehabilitation for perpetrators does not displace victims’ reparations, dilute accountability or turn established wrongdoing into competing opinions?

We reopened our wounds so that truth could lead to justice. We did not hand over permission to tidy the history until everybody looks equally unfortunate. Reconciliation is not the victim agreeing to share a bandage with the knife.

International standards recognise that repairing grave violations requires more than money. The UN Basic Principles identify restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction and guarantees of non-repetition. Public acknowledgement and apology belong within that framework. Where is ours?
 
That is the cheapest item on the whole list. Whatever political discomfort an apology may cause, it cannot outweigh the dignity of the families still waiting for one. 

An apology needs no Trust Fund. Only one honest morning...

Neither the United Seychelles nor the LDS administration has delivered the formal state apology and acknowledgement my family has asked for. I want the State to face us all, acknowledge what happened and accept responsibility. We should be invited in, listened to and asked what remains necessary to repair our lives.

Both had the chance. Neither gets to hide behind the other’s record. Both now look foolish for it. Neither can exclude itself and that is the problem we see today. Instead of making the simplest changes to heal our past and people, everything conveniently just comes back to money and rallies, as it always does with the political class and elites who play us daily!

Money is why compensation is "complex". Money is why timetables vanish. Money is why the public only hears the cherry-picked parts they are comfortable discussing. But this was never only about compensation or missed opportunities. It is ultimately about justice and the actual strength of the law over the state. That is what protects us all from disastrous scenarios that could happen. 

Reconciliation can realistically only live in one place: where the law protects the harmed instead of harming them again. Where is the mercy? Where is the compassion to simply do what is right? Nowhere to be seen, clearly...

Now look at what else came out of State House on 16 October. The Cabinet froze electricity tariffs until the end of 2026, and the Vice-President said this stops a rise of 56 cents a unit. Families need this relief. They also deserve to know how the freeze is financed and what will determine their bills after December.

Another State House announcement published that day described discussions about greater flexibility in the 50 per cent debt-to-GDP target so the country can borrow for a new hospital, a bigger port, a new airport, utilities and renewable energy. Mind you, these are merely proposals right now, not policy. But just notice the speed and the premature mention of "what they might do" and "if they can" messaging. We should stop allowing ourselves to be so easily manipulated. 

For concrete and runways, they will discuss rewriting the nation's borrowing rules in a single meeting. For victims, regulations have been announced, but I am still waiting for a clear account of what will reach my family, through which process and by what date. If the Government can discuss long-term financing for infrastructure, victims deserve an equally serious, costed plan for reparations. Publish the obligations, the funding sources and the dates. How do we move forward otherwise? 

Those are their priorities in one day’s news. When they want something, the rules bend like a coconut palm in the wind. When we want something, the rules turn to granite. A government that can find room to borrow for an airport can surely find the money to repair the families its founder's coup left without fathers. So do not tell me this is about money. It is about who they believe matters...

And when they do spend, watch how clearly the figures can suddenly be explained. Ayra Starr came to headline our independence celebrations. I have no quarrel with her. My questions are for the people signing the bookings. The Vice-President reported SCR35.5 million in expenditure across the anniversary programme, with 339 local suppliers benefiting. That is a published figure with identified beneficiaries. Now give victims the same clarity about our reparations.

And what lasting investment in Seychellois talent will outlive the celebrations? Our artists deserve an industry to grow in. Our families deserve a timetable for justice. But apparently securing a performance date with a high price tag is the easier administrative exercise.

That is clearly what we are apparently meant to be grateful for, all in the name of 50 years of independence and now the continued lines of fake reconciliation with absolute resistance to truth.

That has been the pattern for decades. Our talent is swallowed. So many young Seychellois have no family land to inherit and cannot afford to buy their own. Too many of our sons and daughters drift without direction or guidance, and the world barely knows who we are. Already we are being written down as "Creole people". We are Seychellois. Our Kreol language and culture belong to us. So does our history.

The 16 October Cabinet announcement also covered amendments to the Seychelles Made Act and further policy work on trademarks and intellectual property. We all welcome it. But a trademark protects the label on the jar, not the land the fruit grew on. You cannot hand a family a sticker for their chutney when the orchard was taken from their grandfather and never returned. 

The same Cabinet asked the Industrial Estates Authority to inspect foreign workers' housing and to find government land for purpose-built accommodation. Workers who come to build our country deserve decent beds of course, and I say that without hesitation. But I ask out loud: where is the same urgency, and the same government land, for the Seychellois son who has worked here all his life and still cannot put a roof on a plot of his own?

Without correcting the history, empowerment is just another act and fancy speech, for people with no direction or courage.

And to top it off, the thing I will never let pass. Reconciliation, as some in power seem to understand it, means accepting France-Albert René as the hero who built our nation and our people. My father, Davidson "Son" Chang-Him, was killed at Central Police Station on 5 June 1977, the morning of the coup that brought René to power. He was among the first to fall, and I believe that was meant as a message to every brave soul watching: stand down. 

To ask me to call the founder of that coup the builder of my people is to lie to my face about my own father's short life. I will not reconcile with a lie. I can only reconcile with the truth, and the truth is written in the TRNUC report. A people without a past has no future, and some would be very comfortable if we had neither. Is this how Renéism keeps itself alive, by making sure the suffering never quite ends? Until there is nothing left of us to identify with. I want a clear public explanation of how the Commission will implement the findings, and whether it claims any authority to revisit them.

At election time, they can find our front doors without a map. Afterwards, getting an answer becomes an expedition. Seychelles has not grown. Their willingness to answer has shrunk. We remember who stood in our homes or opened their doors, what they promised, which doors closed and what remains undelivered.

Meanwhile, we victims pay our own medical bills, bury our own brothers and sisters, and grow old in the queue, while politicians and elites move from events to tea parties and photo opportunities like celebrities. Some of us have already died waiting. That is how they treat us. Our parents died without ever knowing the full truth about what happened to their children. Children grew up without fathers and mothers. Families lived through murder, disappearance, imprisonment, torture and exile, and lost homes, livelihoods and dignity. 

The Vice-President speaks of being “fearless in dignity”. Very well. What is that dignity worth if it does not extend to every Seychellois citizen? Where is the fearlessness in facing victims, acknowledging the truth and accepting responsibility? Dignity is not reserved for the government benches. Nor is it a shield for lies and corruption.

None of that is closed because a newspaper says so for the sake of politics. A child who lost a parent in 1977 cannot get those years back or their parent. That is impossible! No compensation replaces a parent either. But justice, recognition and accountability can restore dignity. Closure should not be declared on behalf of victims. It has to actually be lived by them before this can be announced by any officials. That is how we know you're doing a good job.

One year into this administration, the promises of the first hundred days have gone soft like breadfruit left too long on the step. Our headlines make us look out of control to the outside world, and "never again" has become a slogan for anniversaries. They used to rely on Radio Bambou, our island grapevine, to carry their version from Victoria to every village. That echo has broken. 

Today the grapevine carries their contradictions, their invoices/receipts, failures and silences. The people are simply comparing notes. Never again was not only about a coup. It was about our lives, and the value every Seychellois life adds to this country. Our children deserve more than inherited hardship and another promise. Look what five decades have truly done for them...

South Africa offers a warning about unfinished reparations. More than twenty years after its 2003 payment regulations, its government was still trying to reach outstanding beneficiaries. Our people do not have twenty more years. Many of us do not even have five.

So, again, since repetition seems to be the only language that reaches State House, we ask from Anba Langar:

1. How many victims and surviving families have actually received the reparations the TRNUC recommended?
2. How will victims be directly consulted, given written reasons and able to challenge decisions affecting their reparations? Whispering behind closed doors is not consultation.
3. What is the clear timetable for compensation and for every outstanding recommendation?
4. Who has the authority to declare closure on behalf of families still waiting for justice?
5. Who will sit on the Trust Fund’s Board, how much money has actually reached the Fund, how much has been paid out, and when will its accounts be published?
6. What safeguards ensure that rehabilitation for perpetrators does not displace victims’ reparations or weaken accountability?
7. When will the state apologise, in person, to the victims and their families?

Let us not confuse another commission with the delivery of justice. Or confuse political announcements with genuine reconciliation. We certainly should not allow history to be rewritten as though every victim and family has already received what they waited half a century for.

Allow me to put my own position on the record, in my own name, because transparency is something I practise, not something I announce. I belong to no one, and I want nothing from anyone in politics except what the law already owes me. 

I publicly disagree with how this government works: with the work ethic that produces frameworks instead of payments, the integrity it claims and does not show, with the type of morals that let it call a victim's silence closure, and the lies it repeats until they sound like policy. I have nothing to hide and never have. Every letter I received, every meeting I attended, every question left unanswered, I am ready to put on the record. Can State House say the same?

No politician is owed my friendship, forgiveness or loyalty. I will not exchange my family’s dignity for access, photographs or promises. My rights do not depend on whether I like the government, or whether it likes me. We need to stop treating politicians like celebrities. Those who refuse accountability should not expect another mandate. The State’s duty to its victims is not a loyalty scheme.

Our ancestors played the moutya at night, around the fire, because the daylight did not belong to them. The drum carried what the mouth was not allowed to say. We are not in the night anymore, and I do not need a drum. I am Son’s daughter. His life was taken from us on 5 June 1977. His family’s voice remains, stronger than ever.

After all these years, I could wake up defeated. Instead, I wake up more determined. You cannot close a grave you never had the courage to visit. When you are ready to stand in front of us without the cameras and say sorry, we will be here. Until then, I will keep shining a light. And above every one of them, we trust that God will have the final word on the process.

Forty-nine years later, we are not asking for favours. We are asking for justice.

That is what protects us all from disastrous scenarios that could happen.

Now look at what else came out of State House on 16 October. The Cabinet froze electricity tariffs until the end of 2026, and the Vice-President said this stops a rise of 56 cents a unit. Families need this relief. They also deserve to know how the freeze is financed and what will determine their bills after December.

Another State House announcement published that day described discussions about greater flexibility in the 50 per cent debt-to-GDP target so the country can borrow for a new hospital, a bigger port, a new airport, utilities and renewable energy. Mind you, these are merely proposals right now, not policy. But just notice the speed and the premature mention of "what they might do" and "if they can" messaging. We should stop allowing ourselves to be so easily manipulated. 

For concrete and runways, they will discuss rewriting the nation's borrowing rules in a single meeting. For victims, regulations have been announced, but I am still waiting for a clear account of what will reach my family, through which process and by what date. If the Government can discuss long-term financing for infrastructure, victims deserve an equally serious, costed plan for reparations. Publish the obligations, the funding sources and the dates. How do we move forward otherwise? 

Those are their priorities in one day’s news. When they want something, the rules bend like a coconut palm in the wind. When we want something, the rules turn to granite. A government that can find room to borrow for an airport can surely find the money to repair the families its founder's coup left without fathers. So do not tell me this is about money. It is about who they believe matters...

And when they do spend, watch how clearly the figures can suddenly be explained. Ayra Starr came to headline our independence celebrations. I have no quarrel with her. My questions are for the people signing the bookings. The Vice-President reported SCR35.5 million in expenditure across the anniversary programme, with 339 local suppliers benefiting. That is a published figure with identified beneficiaries. Now give victims the same clarity about our reparations.

And what lasting investment in Seychellois talent will outlive the celebrations? Our artists deserve an industry to grow in. Our families deserve a timetable for justice. But apparently securing a performance date with a high price tag is the easier administrative exercise.

That is clearly what we are apparently meant to be grateful for, all in the name of 50 years of independence and now the continued lines of fake reconciliation with absolute resistance to truth.

That has been the pattern for decades. Our talent is swallowed. So many young Seychellois have no family land to inherit and cannot afford to buy their own. Too many of our sons and daughters drift without direction or guidance, and the world barely knows who we are. Already we are being written down as "Creole people". We are Seychellois. Our Kreol language and culture belong to us. So does our history.

The 16 October Cabinet announcement also covered amendments to the Seychelles Made Act and further policy work on trademarks and intellectual property. We all welcome it. But a trademark protects the label on the jar, not the land the fruit grew on. You cannot hand a family a sticker for their chutney when the orchard was taken from their grandfather and never returned. 

The same Cabinet asked the Industrial Estates Authority to inspect foreign workers' housing and to find government land for purpose-built accommodation. Workers who come to build our country deserve decent beds of course, and I say that without hesitation. But I ask out loud: where is the same urgency, and the same government land, for the Seychellois son who has worked here all his life and still cannot put a roof on a plot of his own?

Without correcting the history, empowerment is just another act and fancy speech, for people with no direction or courage.

And to top it off, the thing I will never let pass. Reconciliation, as some in power seem to understand it, means accepting France-Albert René as the hero who built our nation and our people. My father, Davidson "Son" Chang-Him, was killed at Central Police Station on 5 June 1977, the morning of the coup that brought René to power. At election time, they can find our front doors without a map. Afterwards, getting an answer becomes an expedition. Seychelles has not grown. Their willingness to answer has shrunk. We remember who stood in our homes or opened their doors, what they promised, which doors closed and what remains undelivered.

Meanwhile, we victims pay our own medical bills, bury our own brothers and sisters, and grow old in the queue, while politicians and elites move from events to tea parties and photo opportunities like celebrities. Children grew up without fathers and mothers. Families lived through murder, disappearance, imprisonment, torture and exile, and lost homes, livelihoods and dignity.

stories.title: India Hands Over Four Ambulances to Seychelles
stories.description: India handed over four advanced life support ambulances to Seychelles as part of bilateral healthcare cooperation. The publication, dated 11 November 2026, says the handover strengthens that cooperation; it does not specify when the handover took place.

Five ambulances are being handed over to the Seychelles Hospital by the Government of India, as part of its commitment to strengthen the country's emergency medical services.

The donation fulfils a pledge made by Indian Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi to President Dr. Patrick Herminie during the latter's State Visit to India in February 2026, when India committed to providing 10 ambulances to Seychelles.

The ambulances will support emergency healthcare services across the country, with some expected to be stationed at other health centres to improve access to emergency medical assistance. One ambulance will also be allocated to the Seychelles Defence Forces (SDF).

publications.title: ¡EL LORO FANTASMA! 🦜 El loro negro de Seychelles, ave nacional de Seychelles #shorts
publications.text:
¿Sabías esto de esta ave? 😱
El loro negro de Seychelles (Coracopsis barklyi) es el ave nacional de Seychelles y vive únicamente en la isla de Praslin, sobre todo en el bosque de palmeras de la Vallée de Mai. Aunque lo llaman negro, su plumaje es grisáceo y marrón y su pico se aclara durante la época de cría. Se alimenta de frutos de palmeras endémicas, flores del coco de mer, guayaba, papaya, mango y bilimbi, y anida en cavidades profundas de troncos viejos, donde pone de 1 a 3 huevos. Está clasificado como Vulnerable: quedan solo entre 520 y 900 ejemplares, amenazados por las ratas introducidas y la competencia por los huecos de anidación.

Seychelles Government backs UAE candidate for UN Secretary-General

The United Seychelles (US) administration has publicly expressed its preference for Lana Zaki Nusseibeh of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) to become the next Secretary-General of the United Nations.

The endorsement comes at a significant moment in the selection process, with eight candidates competing to succeed António Guterres. Five of the candidates are women, raising the possibility that the United Nations could appoint its first female Secretary-General.

Nusseibeh, a Minister of State at the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs, has taken a leave of absence to concentrate on her campaign.

However, the race remains competitive. Under the UN's informal regional rotation, a candidate from Latin America and the Caribbean is considered a strong possibility to take over the post.

In the latest informal Security Council ballot, held on Thursday 5th November, Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan strengthened her position with 12 encouragement votes, one more than she received in the previous straw poll on 30th October.

Meanwhile, Nusseibeh's candidacy has attracted criticism from civil society groups, while international media have raised questions about the UAE's role in the conflict in Sudan and the atrocities linked to the war.

The Secretary-General is the United Nations' chief administrative officer and one of the most influential figures in international diplomacy. The position, established under the UN Charter in 1945, combines the responsibilities of a diplomat, advocate, civil servant and chief executive.

Although the office has limited direct executive powers, its occupant wields considerable diplomatic influence in shaping the international agenda, mediating conflicts and responding to global crises.

The choice of the next Secretary-General will therefore carry significance well beyond the United Nations itself.

stories.title: SSPCA and Police Discuss Animal-Welfare Cooperation
stories.description: The Seychelles Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals says it met the Commissioner of Police and his team on 10 November 2026 to discuss working together on animal welfare, including drawing on the Police Dog Unit’s experience. The SSPCA also cites animals being poisoned or abandoned and points to community education and more accessible sterilisation as ways to address the problem.

publications.text:
Komisyoner Lapolis Msye Godfra Hermitte ansanm avek Sef Sirentandan Joseph Bibi ek Lenspekter Desire Boniface ki Zofisye Ansarz Dog Unit, in zwenn yer bomaten avek bann reprezantan Seychelles Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (SSPCA).

Sa rankont ti en loportinite pour annan en dyalog lo bann diferan fason ki Lapolis ek lezot partener konsernen i kapab travay ansanm pour promouvwar e asir proteksyon ek sekirite bann zannimo, sirtou bann ki ganny proteze anba lalwa.

Pandan sa diskisyon, Komisyoner Lapolis ti met lanfaz lo lenportans pour etablir en bon kolaborasyon avek lezot lorganizasyon non-gouvernmantal (NGO) ek lazans konsernen dan pei. I ti fer resorti ki i enportan pour tou bann partener travay ansanm koman en sel lekip pour kapab adres pli byen bann ka konplent ek labi kont bann zannimo, e asire ki bann ki responsab i ganny pran aksyon neseser avek zot.

Sa i premye rankont ki Lapolis in fer lo sa size avek SSPCA, e i ekspekte ki lezot rankont pou ganny organize dan lavenir pour kontinyen sa dyalog e ranforsi sa kolaborasyon.

On Tuesday, 10 November, the Seychelles Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (SSPCA) had a very positive meeting with the Commissioner of Police and his team. We thank the Commissioner and his officers for taking the time to listen and discuss how we can work together to improve animal welfare in Seychelles.

The SSPCA is exploring how we can work with the police and draw on the experience of the Police Dog Unit. One of our priorities is to get out into our communities and help children and their parents learn how to care for their pets. Teaching kindness to animals starts at home, and children can carry those lessons with them for life.

Too many animals are still poisoned or abandoned, some left beside rubbish bins. The SSPCA and Pet Haven take in and care for animals that have nowhere else to go. Preventing abandonment and making sterilisation more accessible are two practical ways we can reduce the number of animals that end up needing shelter.

The SSPCA and BeKind organise free and low cost sterilisation clinics when volunteer vets are available. Network for Animals has also helped with sterilisation on La Digue, and we hope they’ll return to support efforts on Praslin and Mahé. Thank you to the vets, volunteers and animal welfare groups who give their time to make this work possible.

This meeting is a positive step forward. You can help by sharing news of free sterilisation clinics and talking with your children about what it means to care for a pet. Let’s be kind to our animals and take care of the environment we all share. 🐾🇸🇨

English translation

Commissioner of Police Mr Godfra Hermitte, Chief Superintendent Joseph Bibi and Inspector Desire Boniface, the officer in charge of the Dog Unit, met yesterday morning with representatives of the Seychelles Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (SSPCA).

The meeting provided an opportunity to discuss how the police and other relevant partners can work together to promote and ensure the protection and safety of animals, particularly those protected by law.

During the discussion, the Commissioner of Police stressed the importance of working closely with non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and relevant agencies across the country. He said all partners should work together as one team to respond more effectively to complaints and cases of animal abuse, and to ensure that appropriate action is taken against those responsible.

This was the first meeting between the police and the SSPCA on this subject. Further meetings are expected to continue the dialogue and strengthen cooperation.

stories.title: Russian-Language Centres Planned With African Partners
stories.description: A Telegram publication dated 28 October 2026 reports that Ano Eurasia and Russian human-rights commissioner Jana Lantratova met representatives of Seychelles and other African countries. It says memoranda and cooperation agreements in education, culture and citizens’ rights were signed, and Russian-language and cultural centres are planned; the publication does not specify which countries signed agreements or where centres will open.

publications.text:
África elige el idioma ruso?

En África, planean abrir centros de lengua y cultura rusa, así como centros bilaterales de apoyo a los compatriotas. 

Ano "Eurasia" y el Comisionado de derechos humanos en la Federación de Rusia, Jana Lantratova, se reunieron con representantes de Malí, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Madagascar, Seychelles y Togo. Se han firmado memorandos y acuerdos de cooperación en el ámbito de la educación, la cultura y la protección de los derechos de los ciudadanos.

"Ano Eurasia tiene una gran experiencia en la implementación de proyectos de infraestructura, sociales y educativos a gran escala, así como en la realización de intercambios juveniles y profesionales. Estamos dispuestos a compartir nuestras experiencias con nuestros socios y a identificar iniciativas que respondan a las necesidades de cada parte. Una parte importante de este trabajo será la apertura de Centros de lengua y cultura rusa. Reunirán a estudiantes, profesores, especialistas y se convertirán en plataformas para el diálogo intercultural entre los jóvenes de nuestros países", dijo el presidente del Consejo de administración de ano Eurasia, Peter Fradkov.
¿Para qué sirve?

Como dicen los representantes de alto nivel de los países africanos: hay un deseo y una demanda entre la población local, especialmente entre los jóvenes, que cada vez más van a recibir educación en las universidades rusas.

El jefe de Rossotrudnichestvo, Igor Chaika, llamó la atención sobre el hecho de que en África ya más de 4500 personas están aprendiendo el idioma ruso sobre la base de las instituciones de la agencia, y también anunció el reclutamiento objetivo y los microperlas.

"También estamos avanzando hacia el principio de reclutamiento objetivo: los estudiantes serán educados en las áreas necesarias para los diferentes sectores de la economía de sus países. Después de graduarse, podrán regresar a su tierra natal y contribuir al desarrollo de su país y al fortalecimiento de las relaciones con Rusia. El próximo año lanzaremos el programa de microgramos. Cualquier persona puede solicitar la implementación de un proyecto conjunto con Rossotrudnichestvo en el marco de la construcción de las relaciones humanitarias internacionales", dijo Chaika.

stories.title: British Indian Ocean Territory Created
stories.description: According to the publication, the British Indian Ocean Territory was created on 8 November 1965, comprising the Chagos Archipelago, Aldabra (Seychelles), Farquhar (Seychelles) and Des Roches (Seychelles) islands.

publications.text:
What happened on November 8!

In 1965, Britain established the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT), bringing several Indian Ocean island groups under a new administrative territory. It initially included the Chagos Archipelago, Aldabra, Farquhar and Des Roches islands, which were separated from Mauritius and Seychelles before their independence. The creation of BIOT was closely linked to Britain's defence arrangements with the United States, which later developed a major military base on Diego Garcia. The decision also led to the displacement of the Chagossian population and decades of political and legal disputes over sovereignty and the right of return.

stories.title: Schools and Government Offices Closed Across Seychelles
stories.description: On 20 October 2026, authorities closed all schools and government offices in Seychelles, except essential services, amid persistent bad weather and landslide danger. The DRDM had warned on 19 October that saturated ground in many parts of the island could lead to landslides, falling trees and localized flooding; La Misère (Seychelles) road remained closed as a safety measure.

publications.text:
**ANY SEYCHELLES, MIJANONA HO MAMPANAHY NY TOETRANDRO**

Noho ny faharetan'ny ratsy ny andro sy ny loza mety hianjeran'ny tany, dia nanambara ny manampahefana fa hikatona avokoa ny sekoly rehetra sy ny sampan-draharaham-panjakana rehetra **androany Talata 20 Oktobra**, afa-tsy ireo sampandraharaha tena ilaina.

Tamin'ny fanambarana navoaka omaly Alatsinainy 19 Oktobra, dia nampitandrina ny Departemantan'ny fitantanana ny loza sy ny loza voajanahary (DRDM) fa tena feno rano ny tany any amin'ny faritra maro ao amin'ny nosy.

Mety hiteraka fianjeran'ny tany, fianjeran'ny hazo ary tondra-drano any an-toerana ny rotsak'orana vaovao.

Noho ny fepetra fiarovana dia mbola mihidy hatramin'ny filazana vaovao ny lalan'i La Misère. Asaina mampiasa lalana hafa sy mitandrina fatratra ny mpamily fiara.

Manoro hevitra ny mponina ihany koa ny manampahefana mba hialana amin'ny dia tsy ilaina, ny asa fanadiovana akaikin'ny tehezan-tendrombohitra tsy marin-toerana ary ny faritra atahorana hianjera.

Mijanona ho vonona ny Foibe nasionaly misahana ny vonjy taitra, ary mbola azo antsoina 24 ora isan'andro ny laharana vonjy taitra 160.
  ✍️: @Top FM mauritice

Aux Seychelles, les conditions météorologiques restent préoccupantes. Face à la persistance des intempéries et aux risques de glissements de terrain, les autorités ont annoncé la fermeture de tous les établissements scolaires et services publics pour ce mardi 20 octobre, à l’exception des services essentiels.

Dans un communiqué publié ce lundi 19 octobre, le Département de gestion des risques et des catastrophes (DRDM) met en garde contre une forte saturation des sols dans plusieurs régions de l’archipel. De nouvelles précipitations pourraient provoquer des glissements de terrain, des chutes d’arbres et des inondations localisées.

Par mesure de sécurité, la route de La Misère reste fermée jusqu’à nouvel ordre. Les automobilistes sont invités à emprunter des itinéraires alternatifs et à faire preuve d’une extrême prudence.

Les autorités recommandent également à la population d’éviter les déplacements non essentiels, les travaux d'excavation à proximité des pentes instables et les zones exposées aux risques d’éboulement.

Le Centre national des opérations d’urgence reste mobilisé, tandis que la ligne d’urgence 160 demeure accessible 24 heures sur 24. La situation fait l’objet d’une surveillance continue et de nouvelles communications officielles seront diffusées en fonction de son évolution.
